title: Nepal floods: Search and rescue operations continue - Islamic Relief Worldwide

full_article:
September 11, 2026 Nepal -

Rescue efforts are still underway in Nepal in the wake of the enormous floods that struck the north of the country 2 weeks ago.

Search and rescue operations are particularly focused around hydropower facilities and tunnels where people are believed to remain trapped.

More than 13,000 people have been rescued so far.

A displacement crisis

Thousands of survivors have seen their homes swept away by the floods and have been forced to relocate to displacement camps. More than 3,600 people are currently living across 37 displacement camps and holding centres, while others are staying with host communities, relatives or other temporary arrangements.

So far, Islamic Relief has delivered close to 1,500 emergency shelter kits to displaced families in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

Each shelter kit includes essential items such as tarpaulins, rope, blankets, pillows, and foam mattresses to help families meet their immediate needs.

We are working with our partners Shelter Box to distribute shelter kits to the flood affected families of Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot district

An unprecedented disaster

It is believed that more than 1.6 million people have been impacted in some way by the floods – approximately 84,000 people are in need of humanitarian assistance.

The latest figures from Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) confirm that 1,367 people have been killed. Another 5,100 are missing.

More than 11,000 hectares of land have been damaged, while about 292,000 livestock have been affected. Damage to agricultural land and livestock is expected to have longer-term implications for household food security and livelihoods.

Collapsed bridges and damaged roads continue to leave remote communities isolated.

Damage to 46 separate water supply systems have left families without reliable access to safe drinking water.

More than 2 weeks after the disaster, the humanitarian situation in Nepal remains critical.

Donate to our Nepal Floods Emergency Appeal today, and help us to deliver more aid to families in Nepal who have had their lives ripped apart by the devastating floods.

ढहल पुल आ क्षतिग्रस्त सड़कक कारण दूरस्थ समुदाय अलग-थलग पड़ल रहैत अछि।

आपदा के २ सप्ताह से अधिक समय बाद भी नेपाल के मानवीय स्थिति गंभीर बनलऽ छै ।

आइये हमर नेपाल बाढ़ि आपातकालीन अपील मे दान करू, आ नेपाल मे जे परिवार विनाशकारी बाढ़ि सँ अपन जीवन फाटि गेल अछि ओकरा बेसी सँ बेसी सहायता पहुँचेबा मे सहयोग करू।

title: Nepal Keeps China-India Competition Out of Its Rescue Efforts - The China-Global South Project
description: Nepal Keeps China-India Competition Out of Its Rescue Efforts  The China-Global South Project

Key Takeaways Kathmandu limited and coordinated foreign SAR teams to prevent China - India rivalry from disrupting rescue operations.

The 18th century founder of modern Nepal, Prithvi Narayan Shah, famously described his new nation as being “like a yam between two boulders.” In his metaphor, China and India were the boulders, and today this dynamic continues to play out in the form of strategic competition for influence in Nepal, which borders both Asian giants.

In the aftermath of the avalanche disaster that triggered a catastrophic flood on August 26 near the Nepal-China border, Kathmandu rushed search-and-rescue (SAR) teams into the debris to find as many of the thousands of missing victims as possible. Despite the scale of the national emergency, Nepal initially declined offers of foreign SAR teams, including from both India and China.

Kathmandu had good reason to be cautious. According to a senior Nepali Foreign Ministry official, the government had learned from its experience following the devastating 2015 earthquake, when the influx of foreign rescue teams—and competition among the countries sending them—created significant coordination and management problems.

The 2015 earthquake demonstrated what Kathmandu hopes to avoid this time around. India and China, alongside other major foreign players such as the U.S., rapidly dispatched rescue personnel and substantial humanitarian assistance, but their responses also became another arena for their broader competition for influence in Nepal.

Following the 2015 disaster, New Delhi launched Operation Maitri and deployed military aircraft, helicopters, medical teams, and rescuers, while Beijing mounted what was then one of its largest overseas humanitarian operations. The resulting competition for visibility and goodwill created practical coordination challenges for an already-overstretched Nepali government.

This time around, Nepal has actively sought to manage the foreign SAR presence, probably to prevent competition from undermining coordination or creating the appearance that Kathmandu favors one nation over another. Indian, Chinese, and South Korean tunnel-rescue specialists have operated in coordination with the Nepali Army, while SAR teams from Australia, Malaysia, and the United Arab Emirates have since joined the effort.

Two weeks after the disaster, Nepal has notably not transitioned entirely from rescue to recovery. On September 8, the government said operations were continuing “while hopes of finding survivors remain,” particularly in hydropower tunnels where workers may have survived in air pockets. Four people were rescued alive between September 4 and 5 alone, including two Nepali workers who survived nine days underground and a Chinese national rescued from another tunnel.

Nepalese leaders have long rejected the idea that Kathmandu should choose between its giant neighbors. Former Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli once put it plainly: “There is no question about aligning with the one or the other. We cannot do it and it is not a viable policy option either.”

Foreign Minister Khanal continued Kathmandu’s tradition of nonaligned foreign policy by noting that “We are effortful to maintain a balanced relationship with all friendly countries, including neighbors India and China.”

Indeed, within his first 100 days in office, Nepal’s current prime minister, Balendra Shah, had been so cautious on this matter that he created a self-imposed rule that while his government could meet individually with diplomatic envoys, it then had to avoid the appearance of favoritism by meeting with the rival ambassador on the same day. Although Shah’s policy of symbolic balance eventually broke down over the summer, Shah’s attempt is a testament to the seriousness with which Nepal takes its nonalignment.

As Nepal’s disaster response has clearly demonstrated, it is not fundamentally opposed to foreign support. Rather, Kathmandu seeks to benefit from foreign support solely on its own terms to avoid unnecessarily antagonizing any partner.

Depending on the circumstances, Nepal could serve as a model on how to deal with intensifying China-India competition for other nations, not just within South Asia, but across the Global South, for years to come. Nepal may remain a yam between two boulders, but Kathmandu is demonstrating that it can still determine how much those boulders shape its fate.

प्रमुख टेकअवे काठमांडू चीन - भारत के प्रतिद्वंद्विता के बचाव कार्य में बाधा नै पहुँचै लेली विदेशी एसएआर टीम के सीमित आरू समन्वय करलकै ।

सीमित आ समन्वित विदेशी एसएआर टीमक कें रोकय कें लेल - प्रतिद्वंद्विता कें बचाव अभियानक कें बाधित करय सं. नेपाल एक असंरेखित, संतुलित कूटनीति कायम रखैत अछि, चीन आ भारत के बीच चुनाव करय सं मना करैत अछि , मात्र अपन शर्त पर सहायता स्वीकार करैत अछि.

एकटा गैर-संलग्न, संतुलित कूटनीति कें कायम रखयत छै, आ कें बीच चयन करय सं मना करयत छै, केवल अपन शर्तक पर सहायता स्वीकार करयत छै. काठमांडू केरऽ ई दृष्टिकोण स॑ ई मॉडलिंग करलऽ जाब॑ सकै छै कि ग्लोबल साउथ राष्ट्र चीन-भारत केरऽ प्रतिस्पर्धा क॑ कोना प्रबंधित करै छै जबकि संप्रभुता क॑ बचाबै छै आरू विदेशी सहायता स॑ लाभ उठाबै छै ।

आधुनिक नेपाल के १८वीं सदी के संस्थापक पृथ्वी नारायण शाह अपन नव राष्ट्र के “दू बोल्डर के बीच के रतालू के तरह” के रूप में प्रसिद्ध रूप स वर्णन केने छलाह | हुनकऽ रूपक म॑ चीन आरू भारत बोल्डर छेलै, आरू आय ई गतिशीलता नेपाल म॑ प्रभाव लेली सामरिक प्रतिस्पर्धा के रूप म॑ खेललऽ जाय रहलऽ छै, जे एशिया केरऽ दोनों दिग्गज के सीमा स॑ सटलऽ छै ।

नेपाल-चीन सीमाक समीप 26 अगस्त कए विनाशकारी बाढ़ि उत्पन्न करय बला हिमस्खलन आपदाक बाद काठमांडू खोज-बचाव (एसएआर) टीम कए मलबा मे दौड़ल गेल ताकि हजारों लापता पीड़ित मे स बेसी स बेसी खोजल जा सकए। राष्ट्रीय आपातकाल केरऽ पैमाना के बावजूद नेपाल न॑ शुरू म॑ भारत आरू चीन दूनू के सहित विदेशी एसएआर टीम केरऽ प्रस्ताव क॑ ठुकरा देलकै ।

काठमांडू के सावधान रहबाक नीक कारण छल। नेपाली विदेश मंत्रालय केरऽ एगो वरिष्ठ अधिकारी के अनुसार सरकार न॑ २०१५ केरऽ विनाशकारी भूकंप के बाद मिललऽ अनुभव स॑ सीखल॑ छेलै, जब॑ विदेशी बचाव दल केरऽ आवागमन – आरू ओकरा भेजै वाला देशऽ के बीच प्रतिस्पर्धा – स॑ समन्वय आरू प्रबंधन म॑ महत्वपूर्ण समस्या पैदा होय गेलै ।

2015 के भूकंप एहि बेर काठमांडू के जे चीज सं बचय के उम्मीद अछि ओकर प्रदर्शन केलक. भारत आरू चीन न॑ अमेरिका जैसनऽ अन्य प्रमुख विदेशी खिलाड़ी के साथ-साथ तेजी स॑ बचाव कर्मी आरू पर्याप्त मानवीय सहायता भेजलकै, लेकिन ओकरऽ प्रतिक्रिया भी नेपाल म॑ प्रभाव लेली ओकरऽ व्यापक प्रतिस्पर्धा लेली एगो आरू अखाड़ा बनी गेलै ।

2015 केरऽ आपदा के बाद नई दिल्ली न॑ ऑपरेशन मैत्री शुरू करी क॑ सैन्य विमान, हेलीकॉप्टर, मेडिकल टीम, आरू बचावकर्मी क॑ तैनात करलकै, जबकि बीजिंग न॑ जे तत्कालीन ओकरऽ सबस॑ बड़ऽ विदेशी मानवीय अभियान म॑ स॑ एक छेलै, ओकरा माउंट करलकै । एकरऽ परिणामस्वरूप दृश्यता आरू सद्भावना केरऽ प्रतिस्पर्धा स॑ पहल॑ स॑ अधिक तनावग्रस्त नेपाली सरकार लेली व्यावहारिक समन्वय चुनौती पैदा होय गेलै ।

एहि बेर नेपाल सक्रिय रूप स विदेशी एसएआर क उपस्थिति कए प्रबंधन करबाक प्रयास केलक अछि, संभवतः एहि लेल जे प्रतिस्पर्धा स समन्वय कए कमजोर नहि होए या काठमांडू एक राष्ट्र कए दोसर राष्ट्र स बेसी पक्षधर अछि। भारतीय, चीनी, आरू दक्षिण कोरिया केरऽ सुरंग-बचाव विशेषज्ञ न॑ नेपाली सेना के साथ समन्वय करी क॑ काम करलकै, जबकि ओकरऽ बाद ऑस्ट्रेलिया, मलेशिया, आरू संयुक्त अरब अमीरात केरऽ एसएआर टीम भी ई प्रयास म॑ शामिल होय गेलऽ छै ।

आपदा के दू सप्ताह बाद नेपाल उल्लेखनीय रूप स॑ बचाव स॑ ठीक होय के तरफ पूरा तरह स॑ संक्रमण नै करलकै । 8 सितंबर क॑ सरकार न॑ कहलकै कि परिचालन जारी छै “जबकि बची गेलऽ लोगऽ के खोज के उम्मीद बनलऽ छै,” खास करी क॑ जलविद्युत सुरंगऽ म॑ जहाँ मजदूर हवाई जेब म॑ बचलऽ हुअ॑ सकै छै । असगरे ४ सँ ५ सितम्बर के बीच ४ गोटेके जिन्दा उद्धार कायल गेल अछि, जाहिमे भूमिगत नौ दिन बचि गेल दू गोटे नेपाली मजदूर आ दोसर सुरंगसँ उद्धार कएल गेल चीनी नागरिक सेहो रहल अछि ।

नेपाली नेता सब बहुत दिन स एहि विचार कए खारिज क रहल छथि जे काठमांडू कए अपन विशाल पड़ोसी मे स एकटा चुनबाक चाही। पूर्व प्रधानमन्त्री के.पी. शर्मा ओली एक बेर एकरा साफ-साफ कहने छलाह: “एक या दोसर के संग तालमेल बनेबा पर कोनो सवाल नहि अछि, हम सब ई काज नहि क सकैत छी आ ई कोनो व्यवहार्य नीतिगत विकल्प सेहो नहि अछि।”

विदेश मंत्री खनाल नँ काठमांडू केरौ गैर-संलग्न विदेश नीति के परंपरा क आगू बढ़ाबैत कहलकै कि “हम पड़ोसी देश भारत आरू चीन सहित सब दोस्त देशौ के साथ संतुलित संबंध बनाबै के प्रयास करी रहलौ छियै।”

सचमुच, अपन कार्यकाल के पहिल सौ दिन के भीतर नेपाल के वर्तमान प्रधानमंत्री बलेन्द्र शाह एहि मामला पर एतेक सावधान भ गेल छलाह जे ओ एकटा स्वंयमय नियम के निर्माण केलखिन्ह जे हुनकर सरकार जखन कि कूटनीतिक दूत सं व्यक्तिगत रूप सं भेंट क सकैत छल, मुदा तखन ओकरा ओही दिन प्रतिद्वंदी राजदूत सं भेंट क पक्षपात के रूप सं बचय पड़ल छल. हालांकि शाह केरऽ प्रतीकात्मक संतुलन केरऽ नीति अंततः गर्मी के दौरान टूटी गेलै, लेकिन शाह केरऽ ई प्रयास नेपाल अपनऽ असंरेखण क॑ जे गंभीरता स॑ लै छै, एकरऽ गवाह छै ।

जेना कि नेपाल केरऽ आपदा प्रतिक्रिया स॑ स्पष्ट रूप स॑ पता चललै कि ई विदेशी समर्थन के मौलिक रूप स॑ विरोध नै करै छै । बल्कि काठमांडू केवल अपन शर्त पर विदेशी सहयोग स लाभ उठाबय चाहैत अछि ताकि कोनो साथी कए अनावश्यक विरोध नहि हो।

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day.

In New York, family members of the victims, many carrying pictures of their loved ones, joined Vice President JD Vance and four former US presidents at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8:46 a.m. ET (1246 GMT) with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Center's North Tower.

Shortly after, victims' family members began reading aloud the names of all 2,977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, a somber recitation that lasts for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.

Other moments of silence followed, marking when the other three airplanes crashed and the two towers collapsed. For the first time, a ‌seventh moment of silence ‌was set to honor the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that ‌poisoned the ⁠air for months ⁠afterward.

Gregory Carafello attended the ceremony to honor the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm that lost more than 650 employees in the attacks. Carafello was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate.

"Everyone should realize that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families," he said. "These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work."

At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building's west flank, killing 184, President Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip.

The president and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which ⁠they have defended as necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

"We salute our first responders and law enforcement, ‌and we love them," Trump said. "And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world's ‌number one sponsor of terror, Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon."

Mourners were also gathering in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down ‌one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.

US President Donald Trump (L) and First lady Melania Trump stand for the national anthem during an official 9/11 observance ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the 11 September attacks, at the Pentagon, in Arlington, Virginia, USA, 11 September 2026. (EPA)

GENERATIONAL PAIN

The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or ‌grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security.

But for many whom the attacks directly affected — the victims' families and friends, first responders and rescue workers — the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter century ago and the heartbreak that followed.

Caroline Ogonowski's father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower.

Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to ‌her father's grave last week and attended a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday.

"This year, there's this new sadness in knowing that they won't ever get to know each other," Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and ⁠humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. "My father ⁠will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather.

"We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it," she added.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani listens to names of victims is read on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, in New York. (AP)

LASTING LEGACY

A generation of Americans has grown up since 2001 who are too young to remember the attacks, but whose lives were fundamentally altered by them.

The attacks initiated the "war on terror," which led to the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump's rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements — a promise being tested by the Iran war.

At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks.

At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colors Americans' perceptions of Muslims to this day. Zohran Mamdani, New York's first Muslim mayor, faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday's ceremony, which he rejected.

Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died.

The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show.

Twenty-six have died this year alone.

description: Nepal calls for international financial compensation following deadly floods  Jurist.org
publisher.title: Jurist.org
full_article:
Nepal on Wednesday appealed for emergency assistance from a UN fund designed to help developing countries cope with the irreversible effects of climate change, as it sought climate justice and floods caused by an August 26 glacier collapse on its border with China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.

Commenting on the gravity of the situation that Nepal is facing, UN Resident Coordinator for Nepal, Lila Pieters Yahia stated:

The devastation Nepal has experienced is an extraordinary, stark illustration of the losses and damages that climate-vulnerable countries are increasingly facing.

Nepal submitted an urgent request to the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The government’s letter stated that as “a least developed and highly climate-vulnerable mountainous country, Nepal contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions yet continues to bear disproportionate and escalating climate impacts.”

The Fund was established at the 27th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP27) in 2022 and operationalized at the 28th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28) in 2023. It is designed to help developing countries respond to climate impacts that cannot be avoided or adapted to. Nepal, whose mountainous terrain makes the country susceptible to melting ice and glacial lake outbursts, was a strong advocate for the Fund’s creation.

The floods have affected 84,270 people. According to the latest update from Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 13,656 people have been rescued, 5,130 remain missing, and 1,377 are confirmed dead.

Nepal and the UN have raised $22 million of a flash appeal for $49.6 million launched last week. The appeal aims to provide direct cash assistance, cold-weather shelter materials, portable solar power units, water purification systems, food aid, and emergency mobile clinics to 84,000 people before the end of the year.

Despite the Fund’s purpose of shifting the burden of climate response away from countries that have contributed least to emissions, pledged amounts fall below projected needs. Only $485.77 million has been received of the $822.71 million pledged. To date, the Fund has not disbursed money to any country.

How the Board responds to Nepal’s request will test whether the Fund can play a meaningful role in climate disaster recovery. By using the language of climate justice, Nepal is pressing the international community to share the financial responsibility for loss and damage caused by climate disasters more equitably.

title: Nepal floods: how measuring snow in the Himalayas could help avoid future disasters - The Conversation
description: Nepal floods: how measuring snow in the Himalayas could help avoid future disasters  The Conversation
publisher.title: The Conversation
full_article:
The massive and deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border are a stark reminder of why the world needs to constantly update its understanding of the fragile ecosystem in the Himalayas.

These towering mountains contain nearly 90,000 glaciers, which sustain ten major river systems. Countries nearby, including India, Pakistan, China, Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan, are reliant on water resources that cross borders here. As major river-based hydro economies, their agricultural production, energy security and wider economic stability depend on the availability and the timing of river flows.

Changes in snowmelt, glacier retreat and water availability can cause untold hardship for millions of people relying on it. It can also create incredible danger as seen in August 2026, when a flash flood caused by a collapsed glacier washed away villages, bridges and roads on both sides of the Tibet-Nepal border, killing more than 1,000 people.

Understanding and measuring winter snowfall in these regions is exceptionally important. It is the main source of freshwater when it is released by snow melting during the region’s warm and early-summer crop growing seasons, when local communities need it most.

Read more: Nepal-Tibet disaster linked to climate change – a glaciologist explains

Understanding future Himalayan hazards

No one knows precisely how much water the mountains currently provide, and how this will change. This knowledge gap also hinders our understanding of the occurrence of geo-hazards including avalanches triggered by extreme snowfall events and flooding caused by the rapid melting of snow.

The recent Nepal disaster could be related to a spell of unusually warm weather. This may have weakened the snowpack creating a rapid melt. I work with a team of glaciologists at the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors six miles (10km) away from the site. Results suggest that enhanced melting could have introduced water into the crevasses weakening the ice-rock connections.

Studies project that roughly half of the glacier ice in the Himalayas (equivalent to about two billion Olympic swimming pools) could melt by the end of this century – enough to raise sea levels by over a centimetre but there is still considerable uncertainty in these projections.

This is because we do not have enough measurements of snowfall and ice across large areas in this challenging terrain. As a result, scientists often have to extrapolate from relatively small numbers of observations to enormous and highly varied terrain.

Computer-based tools (known as models) that combine available observations with information about land and the atmosphere have proved to be indispensable and often come to rescue when gap-filling is necessary. But models are only as good as the observations used to constrain them.

New scientific approaches are beginning to offer solutions, but they are rather sparse and insufficient on their own beyond the region where they have been tested.

For example, my recent study with colleagues found a new way to accurately measure mountain snowfall reducing measurement errors dramatically – measuring snow has been a long-standing problem because of which mountain water resources have been hugely underestimated over the years.

Measuring Himalayan glaciers.

Another regional study recently reported a measure of the water stored in some of the key Nepalese glaciers using an airborne method that involves taking an aerial survey of the region using instruments mounted on a helicopter. Scientists are also using a technique known as radar interferometry, which uses a combination of radio waves to detect very fast-moving mountain slopes that risk collapsing.

A combination of one or more such techniques could be used to predict where snowfall is concentrated, how much water it is likely to contribute to the region and also identify areas at risk. New information could be used to cast early warning preparedness strategies feeding into a forewarning system for timely evacuation of the region’s most vulnerable.

What happens next?

Scientific innovation alone will not be enough. There is an urgent need for proven ideas to be commercially adapted and systematically deployed across critical zones. The numbers and the imminent dangers involved can now no longer be left to discussions in research papers and conferences, they must be made public on the equivalent of a war footing.

An evacuation success story from the Swiss village of Blatten in 2025 shows what this can achieve. Hundreds of people were moved out before a huge section of the glacier broke off. The authorities had already identified areas at risk and publicly shared hazard maps. Continuous monitoring of the landscape, precipitation and ground movement fed into an early warning system.

But success stories from the west cannot simply be transplanted wholesale into the Himalayan context because of the region’s inhospitable elevation, harsh weather and limited infrastructure. An approach that factors in indigenous and traditional knowledge should be part of plans and policies.

What is also needed in the Himalayas is a far more highly coordinated monitoring network that brings together everyone who depends on and manages mountain water. This would include potential state and non-state organisations, researchers, local authorities and mountain communities. Communities should be central to this effort. Local people can help install and maintain monitoring equipment, collect observations and contribute knowledge of their own environment.

Examples of existing successes from the region include the use of community-managed reservoirs to artificially store meltwater, the construction of ice stupas (an artificial glacier) and glacier grafting techniques to grow new, water-producing glaciers designed to gradually release water during the growing season. The community-based flood warning system in parts of Nepal’s Koshi basin is a success story but is limited in its approach to provide alerts during a cascading disaster, such as the one we witnessed recently.

These results should help policymakers and scientists understand how communities dependent on mountain ecosystems are responding to change – and what support they need to adapt to reduce their vulnerability to future hydro-climatic shocks, such as droughts and floods.

Regardless of the current changes in Himalayan snowfall and glacier melt, local people need to play a vital role in helping measure what is happening in the climate system. And that, as well as countries working more closely together, should help with the future planning that is desperately needed.

title: How diaspora groups in the US are responding to disasters in Nepal, Colombia, Venezuela and other homelands - The Conversation
description: How diaspora groups in the US are responding to disasters in Nepal, Colombia, Venezuela and other homelands  The Conversation
publisher.title: The Conversation
full_article:
A string of major disasters in 2026 have had devastating consequences. Earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia and floods and mudslides in Nepal have killed tens of thousands of people and injured many more. Countless people remain missing and hundreds of thousands of homes are damaged, with some entire neighborhoods destroyed.

The responses have been global. For Nepal alone, the United Nations Global Emergency Fund has allocated US$2 million, while the U.S. has committed over $3 million and the European Union has sent just under $3 million. Big humanitarian organizations such as Direct Relief and Save the Children have started fundraising campaigns to support the response efforts in Nepal.

Among the first to respond have been support groups set up by people originally from countries hit by disaster but now living elsewhere.

While small in scale, these diaspora groups are well positioned to respond quickly to disaster relief efforts. They have developed partnerships with community groups on the ground in their home countries. They also have a strong pool of donors – among the diaspora and beyond – based in the U.S.

I study philanthropy and nonprofits and research diaspora-led nonprofits. These organizations play multiple roles. They support other people in their immigrant communities in the U.S. and engage in the preservation of their cultures while living far from their homelands. Increasingly, they also respond to urgent needs in their countries of origin.

Diaspora giving

The money people living abroad send to their relatives and friends back home is called remittances. Globally, more than $900 billion flows across borders annually this way.

Diaspora communities are also playing a growing role in development aid and giving in response to disasters in many countries. This is additional money beyond that $900 billion; no authoritative estimate is available.

The Nepalese diaspora groups that have responded are less visible. But nonprofits led by Nepalese people who live in the U.S., like the Nepali Association of Oregon, the Albany New York Nepalese Society and Nepalese Aid, are gathering donations to send back to their homeland.

Likewise, after the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes, Venezuelans living abroad, including business owners, and organizations led by Venezuelan emigrants, such as Venezuelans and Immigrants Aid, have mobilized.

Nonprofits that can step up quickly

My research shows that diaspora-led nonprofits are able to quickly respond when disasters strike because of the partnerships they have already forged with community groups in their homelands.

For instance, I found that Colombian diaspora-led organizations have ongoing projects in areas that range from education to nutrition. They can ramp up to expand their philanthropy when a disaster occurs.

Give to Colombia, a nonprofit based in Miami-Dade County led by Colombians living there, has swiftly dispatched relief funds before. In November 2020, the Category 4 Hurricane Iota hit Colombia’s Providencia Island. The storm damaged 98% of the island’s infrastructure, and an estimated 40% of the 5,000-plus inhabitants were displaced to other parts of the country.

Organizing with its partners, including the Colombian-based nonprofit Presentes Corporation, Give To Colombia created Stand Up: Providencia Reborn. In 2020, the initiative raised $500,000 to build a community center and reconstruct local inns to help over 1,000 Colombians rebuild their tourism businesses.

Give To Colombia and Presentes Corporation have teamed up again in response to the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck the Chocó region of Colombia on Aug. 10, 2026. Together they have launched Colombia Se Levanta, meaning “Colombia rises up,” to raise money to help pay for recovery and rebuilding efforts.

Venezuelan migrants gather in Detroit on June 28, 2026, to collect humanitarian aid for people affected by the June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela. David Peinado/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Committed volunteers and donors

Most diaspora-led nonprofits have a committed base of volunteers and donors. In the case of the Albany, New York, Nepalese Society, there are more than 600 Nepalese whom the nonprofit is calling on to give in response to the mudslides.

When I studied Mexican hometown associations, I found that those groups typically had anywhere from 20 to 500 active members, with around 3,000 associations in the United States.

I’ve also found that diaspora leaders take pride in their philanthropy.

A Colombian immigrant who helped to create New England Association for Colombian Children in the Boston area told me, “I do not plan on returning to Colombia now, the U.S. is my home. But I get great fulfillment from giving back to the place where I was born.”

She encourages other Colombians living in the U.S. to learn about the organization and to give their time and money to causes in Colombia. As a result, the group has become a magnet for many Colombians who end up in the Boston area.

In addition, diaspora-led organizations deliberately involve young immigrants, whether they came as children to the U.S. or were born to immigrant parents.

This can help expand the donor base of these groups, even when there’s no disaster to respond to. The India Philanthropy Alliance’s annual Youth Essay Competition is a good example of this. It calls on middle and high school students, often Indian Americans, to write essays that identify social challenges facing India and propose solutions.

To be sure, the funds that these diaspora-led nonprofits raise can be modest in comparison to other efforts. Give to Colombia is close to reaching its target of $300,000 in response to Colombia’s 2026 earthquake. The New England Association for Colombian Children also has a campaign underway, Colombia, Estamos Contigo, meaning “We’re with you, Colombia.” It has already surpassed its target of raising $25,000.

Still, I believe these diaspora-led nonprofits have staying power, given the deep sense of connection that they have with their homelands. They will be ready to respond whenever new disasters occur.

The latest figures from Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority show that 1,385 people have died and 5,130 are still missing.

Rescue teams have so far saved 13,676 people. Search and relief operations are continuing in the affected areas.

The government has deployed 21,022 security personnel for rescue and relief work. They include 8,844 Nepal Army personnel, 7,975 Nepal Police personnel and 4,203 Armed Police Force personnel.

Nepal's leaders have said the country needs long term international support to deal with the changing conditions in its mountain regions.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah had earlier said Nepal must “strongly raise” with the international community the disasters it has faced because of climate change.

Shah is expected to travel abroad for the first time as prime minister this month to attend the United Nations General Assembly and raise the issue.

Floods leave widespread destruction

Nepal is a largely rural country with a population of around 30 million. It produces only a small share of the world's greenhouse gas emissions compared with industrialised countries.

The exact reason behind the glacial collapse is still unclear. However, glaciers around the world are melting as global temperatures rise, increasing the risk of such disasters.

Scientists say glaciers in the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are melting faster because of rising temperatures.

Chhetri said the government is now assessing the full damage caused by the disaster.

“Given the scale and extent of the damage, the government is also undertaking a comprehensive post-disaster needs assessment to determine the full extent of loss and damage and the requirement for recovery, rebuilding and reconstruction,” he said.

A preliminary UN assessment estimated damage to buildings from the floods at $158 million. It said the total losses would be much higher after taking into account damage to roads, bridges and farmland, as well as humanitarian costs.

The disaster also caused deaths in neighbouring China. According to state media, 43 people have died and 519 are still missing.

The combined death toll in Nepal and China now stands at 1,428, while more than 5,649 people remain missing. Around 800 foreigners, including tourists and pilgrims, are among those missing.

full_article:
From videos of people fleeing a monstrous wave crashing on a border building in Tibet to aerial shots of devastation along Nepal’s Trishuli river to chilling accounts from survivors, AFP's coverage of the deadly Nepal-China floods is testament to its commitment to accurate, swift, on-the-ground coverage.

Teams in Nepal mobilised instantly, allowing AFP to transmit the first drone shots depicting the unprecedented scale of the disaster to clients swiftly after Kathmandu police confirmed a major flood.

Our correspondents, photographers and video journalists worked through harrowing conditions and constant threat of new flooding, braving kilometres of quick-sand-like mud to bring voices and images from the disaster zones to the world.

Many of their stories were of destruction and despair, as they witnessed ruined homes and accompanied family members giving DNA samples for identification of victims.

But there were also tales of hope and salvation, as rescuers pulled out mud-caked survivors days after the floods.

While access to the Tibet side of the disaster zone was limited, our teams obtained valuable footage of the moment the tsunami-like wave hit. They also reached families of the missing in Tibet, enriching the official coverage from China that focused on the rescue efforts.

Bureaux outside Asia brought stories from relatives of loved ones who had gone missing during their travels, allowing AFP to piece together a picture of the victims -- from residents to hikers to pilgrims.

Our science specialists quickly explained the sequence of the glacial collapse while our factchecking teams verified or debunked many posts online, contributing to the fight against disinformation during the major disaster.

Nepal has estimated that rebuilding after deadly floods triggered by a glacial mountain collapse last month will cost about $4.78 billion, the country’s foreign ministry said on Friday.

The August 26 disaster, which began with a tsunami-like flood on the China-Nepal border, has killed more than 1,400 people and left more than 5,600 missing.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has said that the number of confirmed deaths in the country had risen to 1,385, with 5,130 people still missing.

Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said Prime Minister Balendra Shah would address the UN General Assembly later this month to draw international attention to the repeated loss of life and property caused by climate-related disasters.

Foreign ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said about $57.67 million would be needed for short-term recovery over the next six months, while $4.71 billion would be required for longer-term reconstruction.

Damage assessment

The government is conducting a comprehensive post-disaster assessment to determine the full scale of damage and the needs for recovery and rebuilding, Chhetri said.

A preliminary UN assessment put building damage at $158 million, warning that losses including damage to roads, bridges and farmland, as well as humanitarian costs, would be much higher.

full_article:
Nepal presents the developed world with moral imperative. Act now -- stop climate change. A warming Himalayan glacier broke off at 17,000 feet above sea level and plunged to the valley below in Nepal-- creating incomprehensible destruction. These people contributed nothing to climate change -- and were destroyed by it.

We didn't know at the beginning of the Industrial Revolution that human activities would warm the planet. Now we know. There is no denying advances brought by the revolution. But science tells us there are vast unintended consequences with which we must deal.

In Iowa, we have oppressive heat and humidity, and agricultural implications. The Southwest U.S. wants water; the Colorado River offers little. In Europe, where only 20% of households have air conditioning, an estimated 35,000 people died of heat waves in 2026 (Google it). Drought increases migration that strains goodwill in host countries. Maybe most eerie: the polar ice caps are melting.

Tell Congress and political candidates: No excuse is adequate for spineless inaction.

Linda Svoboda

Cedar Rapids

title: About 70 Americans Unaccounted for After Nepal Disaster - INDIA New England News
description: About 70 Americans Unaccounted for After Nepal Disaster  INDIA New England News
publisher.title: INDIA New England News
full_article:
Washington — About 70 Americans remain unaccounted for in the Nepal-China border region after a disaster destroyed roads, bridges and entire villages, according to the U.S. State Department.

Eighteen Americans had reached safety as of noon Thursday, the department said.

“The safety of Americans in the affected area remains our highest priority,” a State Department spokesperson said. “Despite the significant operational challenges, we are using every available means to locate, account for and assist U.S. citizens and their families.”

The department’s team in Kathmandu has met with all families who traveled to Nepal, while consular officers in Washington have remained in regular contact with families in the United States.

“The conditions responders are operating in within Nepal are extraordinarily difficult,” the spokesperson said. “This disaster destroyed roads, bridges, entire villages, and, in some areas, completely altered the landscape – some previously inhabited places are covered by displaced soil and rocks several feet deep.”

Helicopter operations have also been hampered by the destruction, with pilots flying through narrow valleys where roads, riverbanks and other familiar landmarks have disappeared.

The thin air at high altitude has made some missions extremely dangerous or impossible, according to the spokesperson.

The United States offered to support search-and-rescue operations on the first day of the emergency, but Nepal’s government initially declined the offer after determining that its own agencies could handle the response.

“The United States offered to support search-and-rescue operations on day one; however, the Nepali government declined our initial offer and determined that its own government could handle search-and-rescue operations,” the spokesperson said.

“Eventually, under international pressure, it let several foreign teams in to assist with specialised rescue in hydropower tunnels.”

About 5,100 people remained reported missing across the wider disaster area, according to the department.

“This is a rapidly evolving operation, and we are working closely with our local partners on the ground to adapt to conditions as they change,” the spokesperson said. (Source: IANS)

title: Nepal floods: How measuring snow in the Himalayas could help avoid future disasters - Phys.org
description: Nepal floods: How measuring snow in the Himalayas could help avoid future disasters  Phys.org
publisher.title: Phys.org
full_article:
Credit: Imad Clicks from Pexels

The massive and deadly floods on the Nepal–Tibet border are a stark reminder of why the world needs to constantly update its understanding of the fragile ecosystem in the Himalayas.

These towering mountains contain nearly 90,000 glaciers, which sustain 10 major river systems. Nearby countries, including India, Pakistan, China, Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan, rely on water resources that cross borders here. As major river-based hydro economies, their agricultural production, energy security and wider economic stability depend on the availability and timing of river flows.

Changes in snowmelt, glacier retreat and water availability can cause untold hardship for millions of people who rely on them. They can also create incredible danger, as seen in August 2026, when a flash flood caused by a collapsed glacier washed away villages, bridges and roads on both sides of the Tibet–Nepal border, killing more than 1,000 people.

Understanding and measuring winter snowfall in these regions is exceptionally important. It is the main source of freshwater when released by melting snow during the region's warm, early-summer crop-growing seasons, when local communities need it most.

Understanding future Himalayan hazards

No one knows precisely how much water the mountains currently provide or how this will change. This knowledge gap also hinders our understanding of geohazards, including avalanches triggered by extreme snowfall events and flooding caused by rapid snowmelt.

The recent Nepal disaster could be related to a spell of unusually warm weather. This may have weakened the snowpack, creating rapid melt. I work with a team of glaciologists at the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10 km) from the site. Results suggest that enhanced melting could have introduced water into the crevasses, weakening the ice-rock connections.

Studies project that roughly half of the glacier ice in the Himalayas (equivalent to about 2 billion Olympic swimming pools) could melt by the end of this century—enough to raise sea level by more than 1 centimeter. But there is still considerable uncertainty in these projections.

This is because we do not have enough measurements of snowfall and ice across large areas of this challenging terrain. As a result, scientists often have to extrapolate from relatively small numbers of observations to enormous and highly varied terrain.

Computer-based tools (known as models) that combine available observations with information about land and the atmosphere have proved indispensable and often come to the rescue when gap-filling is necessary. But models are only as good as the observations used to constrain them.

New scientific approaches are beginning to offer solutions, but data remain rather sparse and insufficient on their own beyond the regions where they have been tested.

For example, my recent study with colleagues found a new way to accurately measure mountain snowfall, dramatically reducing measurement errors. Measuring snow has been a long-standing problem, which has led mountain water resources to be hugely underestimated over the years.

Another regional study recently reported a measure of the water stored in some of the key Nepalese glaciers using an airborne method involving an aerial survey of the region using instruments mounted on a helicopter. Scientists are also using a technique known as radar interferometry, which uses a combination of radio waves to detect very fast-moving mountain slopes at risk of collapsing.

A combination of one or more such techniques could be used to predict where snowfall is concentrated, how much water it is likely to contribute to the region and areas at risk. New information could inform early warning preparedness strategies, feeding into a forewarning system for the timely evacuation of the region's most vulnerable people.

What happens next?

Scientific innovation alone will not be enough. There is an urgent need for proven ideas to be commercially adapted and systematically deployed across critical zones. The numbers and imminent dangers involved can no longer be confined to discussions in research papers and conferences. They must be made public on the equivalent of a war footing.

An evacuation success story from the Swiss village of Blatten in 2025 shows what this can achieve. Hundreds of people were moved out before a huge section of the glacier broke off. The authorities had already identified areas at risk and publicly shared hazard maps. Continuous monitoring of the landscape, precipitation and ground movement fed into an early warning system.

But success stories from the West cannot simply be transplanted wholesale into the Himalayan context because of the region's inhospitable elevation, harsh weather and limited infrastructure. An approach that factors in indigenous and traditional knowledge should be part of plans and policies.

What is also needed in the Himalayas is a far more highly coordinated monitoring network that brings together everyone who depends on and manages mountain water. This would include state and nonstate organizations, researchers, local authorities and mountain communities. Communities should be central to this effort. Local people can help install and maintain monitoring equipment, collect observations and contribute knowledge of their own environment.

Examples of existing successes from the region include the use of community-managed reservoirs to artificially store meltwater, the construction of ice stupas (an artificial glacier) and glacier grafting techniques to grow new, water-producing glaciers designed to gradually release water during the growing season.

The community-based flood warning system in parts of Nepal's Koshi basin is a success story, but it is limited in its ability to provide alerts during a cascading disaster, such as the one we witnessed recently.

These results should help policymakers and scientists understand how communities dependent on mountain ecosystems are responding to change—and what support they need to adapt and reduce their vulnerability to future hydroclimatic shocks, such as droughts and floods.

Regardless of the current changes in Himalayan snowfall and glacier melt, local people need to play a vital role in helping measure what is happening in the climate system. That, along with countries working more closely together, should help with the desperately needed future planning.
